messages:
maya: quick spike proposal — i sketched two options for private cp egress: consolidated egress bridge (single per-region bridge owned by CP) vs multiplexed per-tenant relay (lightweight per-tenant relays). want quick tradeoff check before i write RFC :wave:
anil: curious — what's the primary constraint driving this? latency, egress IP preservation, ops complexity?
maya: all of the above but especially: 1) preserve customer source addr where needed, 2) minimize cross-vpc hairpin and NAT costs, 3) keep CP isolation for private deploys.
kira: can you summarize the two patterns briefly?
maya: sure — consolidated egress bridge: one or small set of region-scoped bridges that terminate customer dataplane connections and do egress to the internet or partner endpoints. pros: single place to optimize caching, TLS, outbound pooling; easier to monitor and apply DDoS mitigations. cons: larger blast radius, may need source addr SNAT, per-customer routing harder.
maya: multiplexed relay: each tenant (or cohort) gets a lightweight relay inside their VPC (or customer-managed VPC) that handles egress. pros: preserves source, smaller blast, per-tenant policies. cons: more control plane churn, harder to push global egress features, more ips to manage.
samir: sounds familiar. what about cost model? does consolidated save infra e.g., fewer NLBs, less NAT gateway use?
dave: consolidated reduces NLB count and NATs but introduces higher egress NAT throughput at those nodes. could reduce cross-vpc NAT egress (if we avoid hairpin by routing through bridge), but if bridge is remote it adds RTT.
anil: what about failover semantics? if a consolidated bridge for region fails, many customers impacted. can we do multi-az redundant bridges + per-tenant fallback to relay?
maya: yes, fallback is in the sketch: primary route -> consolidated bridge; on health fail -> per-tenant relay or alternate region. requires healthy probe and policy.
kira: operationally, how do we manage TLS certs and identity for consolidated bridge across many customers (private deployments)?
samir: probably mTLS with per-tenant certs or short-lived client certs. consolidated must authenticate tenant and propagate identity downstream. more surface area but doable with standard mTLS + SNI.
dave: quick note: traffic engineering gets tricky. consolidated needs careful per-tenant queuing/acl to prevent noisy neighbor. otherwise one customer can saturate the bridge.
maya: exactly. we can apply token-level shaping in CP before egress, but that couples CP quota logic with dataplane egress.
anil: can we quantify expected throughput per region for Q3? ballpark numbers help pick thresholds.
maya: rough: 2–3 p95 peaks around 40 Gbps per busy region across customers on hosted tier. dedicated customers will push additional 10–100 Gbps but usually reserved via Dedicated. consolidated for hosted only maybe manageable.
kira: what about IP exhaustion and IP rotation? consolidated means we control fewer egress IPs (good for allowlists) but need rotation plan. per-tenant relays give customers a stable egress IP inside their VPC.
samir: for compliance customers who require static IPs, per-tenant relay is better. consolidated could offer reserved egress IP per customer but that undermines the benefit unless we create many IPs.
dave: on rollout: could start consolidated for new hosted customers, while offering an opt-in relay for compliance ones. over time, if load grows, split bridge by cohort.
anil: any security differences? consolidated centralizes attack surface; more DDoS mitigations possible there. relays distribute risk but harder to detect global patterns.
maya: wanted to highlight a subtle control-plane boundary: if bridge applies per-request token billing/route decisions, it must contact CP for policy. that adds dependency/higher coupling. If relays are more stateless and rely on cached policy, they can survive CP outages better.
kira: can we do a hybrid: keep a consolidated bridge for observability and heavy ops features, but run a lightweight egress datapath in-customer that handles keepalive and source-preservation, tunnelling only when needed?
samir: like a split-proxy: local egress path for basic flows, tunneled to consolidated for features (eval, caching). interesting but more complex routing.
dave: example flow: customer request -> local relay (preserve src) -> if request matches caching policy -> tunnel to consolidated bridge via gRPC stream; else exit locally. policies pushed via xDS.
maya: exactly. pushing policy via xDS + snapshots seems easiest. quick config example I mocked:
```yaml
# egress-bridge policy snippet
- match: domain: example.com
  action: tunnel_to_bridge
  qos: medium
- match: domain: auth.partner
  action: local_exit
  preserve_source: true
```

anil: that hybrid looks promising. rollout complexity is the main downside. we need feature flags and canary by tenant. infra-bot can automate canary deploys.
infra-bot: scheduled canary: bridge-v1 -> staging at 3243057000, rollout window 1h. monitor: egress-p95, nat-errors, tcp-resets.
kira: on metrics — need per-tenant egress p95, nat-snat-count, tunnel-latency, and per-bridge cpu/net.
samir: also track policy-cache-miss-rate on relays (how often they hit CP). high miss means too many roundtrips.
maya: next steps: i'll draft RFC with: diagrams for consolidated, relay, hybrid; failure modes table; rollout plan + canary; config schema (xDS snippet above); cost model. please add short notes here if you have strong opinions.
dave: add a section on queuing and backpressure semantics — abuse protection is important.
anil: include required CP->dataplane heartbeat and offline policy caching strategy.
kira: we should call out compliance customers and recommend per-tenant relay as default for Private.
samir: +1. also include list of tests: NAT leak detection, egress-ip-stability, cross-az failover.
maya: awesome — thanks all. i'll post RFC draft by EOD tomorrow and tag you. :thumbsup:
